newsitem.title: THAILAND: Hun Sen seen having it his way in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen seen having it his way in Cambodia.

text.p: Strongman Hun Sen is firmly in charge of Cambodia after ousting First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, and resistance from the losers will soon taper off, Thai military analysts said on Monday.

The royalists' morale was low after military setbacks dealt them by forces loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen and because Ranariddh was in France during the weekend fighting, the analysts told Reuters.

"Having learnt that Ranariddh will be abroad for some time, they are finding that there is no use in continuing to fight. So we expect resistance from Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC forces will be minimal," said a Thai general monitoring the Cambodia conflict.
Foreign countries were also declining to provide assistance to the warring factions. "So, without the boss, without money, how can anyone continue fighting," the general said.

"The situation in Cambodia will be back to normal within this week because Hun Sen has taken total control of the situation both in military and political aspects," another Thai military source predicted.
Hun Sen's troops were in complete control of Phnom Penh after two days of fighting in the city and its outskirts.
"Everything is over," said General Tom Sombol, a senior Ranariddh commander.

Thai military analysts said Hun Sen, having made major military gains, would now try to lure members of the divided FUNCINPEC to his side, replace Ranariddh as co-premier with a puppet and keep the coalition government in name.

"Many prominent figures in FUNCINPEC are now siding with Hun Sen. We believe that the coalition will continue and Hun Sen might choose one of these FUNCINPEC figures to replace Ranariddh," the military source said.
Reuters correspondent Katya Robinson, reporting from Phnom Penh, quoted political analysts as saying that Hun Sen's takeover was a coup despite his efforts to legitimise his ouster of Ranariddh.

Hun Sen announced on national radio late on Sunday that Ranariddh no longer was Cambodia's first prime minister. But he said the coalition government would continue and called on FUNCINPEC to nominate Ranariddh's replacement.
"It's definitely a coup d'etat, even if Hun Sen can find people to stand in for his coalition partner," said a United Nations official.

A Cambodian political analyst said Hun Sen was "trying to keep the same structure but give himself much more power than he had before. It's completely unconstitutional. It's a coup, but not in a traditional form. It's a modern form of coup."
Analysts said the Khmer Rouge movement, responsible for the 1975-79 "killing fields" regime, was being used as an excuse for Hun Sen to take power.
"If Hun Sen was really looking for Khmer Rouge soldiers, he would do that by lawful means and not by sending shells through people's houses," the U.N. official said.
One Thai military source in Bangkok said Hun Sen would likely retain the coalition government his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) has with FUNCINPEC until the election planned for next May.

"Now Hun Sen is totally in an advantageous position. So he will definitely hold the election next year as planned in order to avoid international pressure on him, and he will be the victor of that poll," he added.

Hun Sen and Ranariddh formed an uneasy coalition after the U.N.-organised 1993 election. Their bickering came to a head at the weekend as Hun Sen, angered by Ranariddh's wooing of former Khmer Rouge hard-liners, unleashed his forces and took control.

Hun Sen, who defected from the Khmer Rouge in 1978 to the Vietnamese-installed government of Cambodia, is a bitter enemy of former Khmer Rouge political leader Khieu Samphan and the group's former foreign minister, Ieng Sary.
Thai military sources said they now expect Ranariddh's forces to team up with former Khmer Rouge strongmen such as Khieu Samphan to wage a war of resistance against Hun Sen.
Khieu Samphan, apparently preparing for the May election, declared over the weekend he had broken from reviled Khmer Rouge supremo Pol Pot and would abide by the country's constitution.
The Thai sources said some pro-Ranariddh generals had met over the weekend at the Thai-Cambodia border to plan resistance strategies against Hun Sen but reached no conclusion.
